subject: chemistry
title: Ionic bonding
key_idea: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Metals lose electrons to form cations and non-metals gain electrons to form anions. The ions pack into a giant lattice, and this explains the properties of ionic compounds.

blocks.text: Ions form when atoms lose or gain electrons to reach a full outer shell. This section covers how ions form and how to draw them.

items.meaning: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons.
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains electrons.

items: Metals lose their outer electrons to form cations, for example Na → Na⁺ + e⁻.
Non-metals gain electrons to form anions, for example Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.
The charge on a simple ion follows from the group: group 1 gives 1+, group 2 gives 2+, group 13 gives 3+, group 15 gives 3−, group 16 gives 2− and group 17 gives 1−.
The number of electrons lost by one atom equals the number gained by the others, so the compound is neutral overall.
Draw only the outer shell of each ion, and put square brackets round it with the charge at the top right.
Show the electrons from one atom as dots and from the other as crosses.
A cation shows the full shell beneath the one it lost. An anion shows eight electrons in its outer shell, including those it gained.
In NaCl, Na gives one electron to Cl. Both ions now have eight electrons in the outer shell.
In MgO, Mg gives two electrons to O. In CaF₂, Ca gives one electron to each of two F atoms.
Metals form cations by losing electrons. Non-metals form anions by gaining electrons.
The group number gives the charge on a simple ion.
The total positive charge equals the total negative charge in the formula.

sections.heading: The giant ionic lattice and bond strength

blocks.text: In a solid, ions are arranged in a regular pattern called a lattice. This section covers the lattice and what makes ionic bonding stronger or weaker.

items: Each ion is attracted to all the oppositely charged ions around it, in all directions.
In sodium chloride each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions, and each Cl⁻ ion by six Na⁺ ions.
The lattice is called a **giant ionic lattice** because the pattern repeats in three dimensions without end.
The formula shows the simplest ratio of ions, for example NaCl, MgO and CaF₂.
A higher ionic charge gives a stronger attraction between the ions.
A smaller ionic radius lets the ions get closer together, so the attraction is stronger.
MgO has Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, which are smaller and more highly charged than the ions in NaCl, so its ionic bonding is stronger and its melting point is much higher.
A giant ionic lattice has strong attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
Bonding is stronger with higher charge and smaller ions.

blocks.text: The size of an ion depends on its number of electron shells and the pull of its nucleus. This section covers the trends in ionic radius.

items: Down a group, ionic radius increases because each ion has an extra electron shell.
Across a period, atomic radius decreases because the nuclear charge increases while the shielding stays about the same, so the outer electrons are pulled in.
A cation is smaller than its atom because it has lost electrons, usually its whole outer shell, and the same protons now pull fewer electrons.
An anion is larger than its atom because it has gained electrons and the electron repulsion increases.

blocks.text: Isoelectronic ions have the same number of electrons. N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ all have ten electrons.

items: They have the same electron arrangement and the same shielding.
From N³⁻ to Al³⁺ the number of protons increases, so the nuclear attraction on the electrons increases.
The ionic radius therefore decreases from N³⁻ to Al³⁺.
Ionic radius increases down a group because of extra shells.
For isoelectronic ions, more protons means a smaller ion.

blocks.text: The properties of ionic compounds follow from the lattice. This section covers the properties and the evidence that ions exist.

rows: Strong electrostatic attraction in all directions needs a lot of energy to overcome.
A blow shifts layers so that ions of the same charge line up and repel, and the lattice splits.
The ions are held in fixed positions, so no charge can flow.
The ions are free to move and carry the charge.
Polar water molecules attract the ions and pull them out of the lattice.

items: The physical properties above, such as high melting points and conduction only when molten or dissolved, fit a lattice of ions.
Migration of ions: when a coloured ionic compound is placed on damp filter paper with a voltage across it, the coloured ion moves towards the electrode of opposite charge.
For example, purple MnO₄⁻ ions move towards the positive electrode, and blue Cu²⁺ ions move towards the negative electrode.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Sort the ionic substances into those that conduct electricity and those that do not.

items: Ionic compounds conduct only when the ions can move: molten or dissolved.
Properties and the migration of coloured ions are evidence for ions.

checks.q: Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride.
checks.a: The Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions have higher charges and are smaller than Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The electrostatic attraction between the ions is stronger, so more energy is needed to overcome it.

checks.q: Explain why the ionic radius decreases from O²⁻ to Mg²⁺.
checks.a: The ions are isoelectronic, with the same number of electrons and shielding. Mg²⁺ has more protons, so the nuclear attraction on the electrons is greater and the ion is smaller.

checks.q: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
checks.a: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move. When molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.

blocks.text: You must know the formulas of compound ions and be able to construct the formula of an ionic compound.

items: Balance the charges so that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
Use brackets round a compound ion when you need more than one, for example Al₂(SO₄)₃ and Mg(OH)₂.
Describe the ionic bonding in sodium chloride (Na⁺ and Cl⁻), magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻) and calcium fluoride (Ca²⁺ and two F⁻).
Dot-and-cross diagrams cover ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding together, so practise drawing all three.
Radius trends are asked for across a period as well as down a group. Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period.
Across Period 3, the cations get smaller from Na⁺ to Al³⁺ and the anions get smaller from P³⁻ to Cl⁻. Each anion is larger than each cation, because it has an extra shell of electrons.
